title: Cricketing great accuses English club of ‘contributing to Indian casualties’ by signing Pakistan player
content:
One of India’s greatest ever cricketers has criticised the decision of an English team to sign a Pakistan international, claiming it could indirectly contribute to the death of Indian soldiers and civilians.

Sunil Gavaskar, who scored a then record 10,122 runs over a 16-year Test career which ended in 1987, has accused the Indian-owned Sunrisers Leeds, a franchise in the English competition The Hundred, of “contributing to the Indian casualties” by funding arms and weapons for Pakistan through the money Abrar Ahmed, a legspin bowler, will pay through tax.

Sunrisers, formerly known as Northern Superchargers, are run by the Sun Group, a media organisation founded by Kalanithi Maran whose daughter, Kaviya, was present at the Hundred auction last week.

They are also the owners of the Sunrisers Hyderabad franchise in the Indian Premier League. They paid £190,000 ($254,000) to sign the 27-year-old spin bowlers in last week’s auction in London — the first of its kind in a major UK sport.

“Ever since the Mumbai attacks in November 2008, Indian franchise owners have simply ignored Pakistani players for the IPL,” Gavaskar wrote in his column for Mid-Day, the Indian newspaper.

“Although belated, the realisation that the fees that they pay to a Pakistani player, who then pays income tax to his government, which buys arms and weapons, indirectly contributes to the deaths of Indian soldiers and civilians, is making Indian entities refrain from even considering having Pakistani artistes and sportspersons.

“Whether it is an Indian entity or an overseas subsidiary of the entity that is making the payment, if the owner is Indian, then he or she is contributing to the Indian casualties. It’s as simple as that.”

Sunrisers Leeds’ purchase of Ahmed, who has represented his country 64 times across formats, was considered a surprise given it followed reports before the auction that The Hundred’s four Indian-owned franchises would not sign Pakistani players amid raised political tensions between the neighbouring countries.

The tensions date back to the partition of the nations in the 1940s, and there was a brief armed conflict in 2025. The relationship often leads to issues in cricket, where the nations rarely play each other in international games outside major global tournaments. Pakistan players have unofficially been excluded from the IPL since 2009, with the two countries having not competed in a bilateral series since 2012-13.

Sunrisers Leeds’ head coach Daniel Vettori, the former New Zealand captain, insisted after last week’s auction that the franchise made bidding decisions based purely on players’ cricketing ability.

“Daniel Vettori, the coach of the team in The Hundred who hails from New Zealand, may not understand this simple dynamic and so may have wanted some Pakistani players in his team, but surely the owner should have had an understanding of the situation and discouraged the purchase,” added Gavaskar.

“Is winning a tournament in a format that no other country plays in much more important than Indian lives?”

Gavaskar, a former India captain and opening batter, was the first player to pass 10,000 Test runs and, in 1983, eclipsed Sir Don Bradman’s record of 29 centuries in that form of the game. He ended his Test career with a batting average of 51.12, with a top score of 236 not out from his 34 hundreds. The 76-year-old remains one of the most prominent figures in Indian cricket.

The England and Wales Cricket board, which runs The Hundred, declined to comment. The Athletic has contacted the SunRisers franchise for a response.
